s: The LORD commands Moses and Aaron to demand that Pharaoh let his people go, and sends frogs, lice, and swarms of flies when he refuses. He answers Moses' prayers by removing the frogs and flies, and sets apart the land of Goshen from the flies so that Pharaoh will know he is the LORD on the earth.

Moses delivers the LORD's demands to Pharaoh and lets Pharaoh set the time for the frogs to be removed. He prays and the frogs die and later the flies depart, and he rejects sacrificing in Egypt, insisting on a three days' journey into the wilderness. He warns Pharaoh not to deal deceitfully again.

Pharaoh asks Moses to entreat the LORD about the frogs and the flies, promising to let the people go to sacrifice, and offers a compromise of sacrificing in the land and then not going very far. Each time relief comes he hardens his heart and refuses to let the people go, even after the magicians tell him the lice are God's finger.
Aaron stretches out his hand with his rod over the waters so frogs come up over Egypt. He also strikes the dust of the earth with his rod, turning it into lice throughout the land.

The land of Egypt is covered with frogs, which die in heaps and make the land stink, then is afflicted with lice on man and animal, and finally corrupted by swarms of flies in the houses of Pharaoh and his servants. Its magicians can imitate the frogs but not the lice, and the Egyptians are said to hold certain sacrifices as an abomination.

The LORD's people are the ones Pharaoh is told to let go so they may serve him, and Moses says they will go three days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice. Their land of Goshen is set apart from the flies as a division between them and Pharaoh's people.

The frogs come up from the rivers, streams, and pools at Aaron's gesture and fill houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens, and kneading troughs. The magicians also produce frogs, but at Moses' prayer the frogs die in houses, courts, and fields and are gathered into stinking heaps, after which Pharaoh hardens his heart.

The lice come when Aaron strikes the dust with his rod, and all the dust of the land becomes lice on man and animal. The magicians try but cannot produce lice and say it is God's finger, yet Pharaoh's heart stays hardened.

The LORD announces swarms of flies that will fill the houses of the Egyptians and the ground, while Goshen is spared. The flies grievously corrupt the land, Pharaoh bargains, and the LORD removes them at Moses' prayer so that not one remains, but Pharaoh again refuses to let the people go.

In Exodus chapter 9, the LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh with a demand to let the Hebrews go, and Pharaoh's refusal brings three more plagues on Egypt. A pestilence kills all of Egypt's livestock while sparing Israel's, then ashes sprinkled by Moses become boils on people and animals, including the magicians. The LORD then warns of an unprecedented hail and tells Pharaoh he was raised up to show God's power, and the hail strikes Egypt's fields, people, animals, flax, barley and trees but spares Goshen. Pharaoh confesses sin and promises to release Israel, but once Moses stops the hail he hardens his heart again and refuses, as the LORD had said.

The LORD demands through Moses that Pharaoh let his people go, and sends the livestock pestilence, the boils and the hail on Egypt while distinguishing Israel from Egypt. He tells Pharaoh that he raised him up to show his power so that his name is declared throughout the earth. He hardens Pharaoh's heart, as he had spoken to Moses.

Moses carries the LORD's warnings to Pharaoh, sprinkles furnace ashes toward the sky to produce the boils, and stretches out his rod toward the heavens when the hail comes. When Pharaoh pleads, Moses leaves the city, spreads his hands to the LORD and the thunder and hail stop. He tells Pharaoh that he does not yet fear the LORD God.

Pharaoh sees that none of Israel's livestock died yet remains stubborn, and he refuses to let the people go after the boils. After the hail he confesses, "I have sinned this time," calls the LORD righteous and promises to release Israel. When the hail ceases he sins yet more and hardens his heart again, along with his servants.
The Israelites, called the children of Israel, are spared the livestock pestilence, as not one of their livestock dies. No hail falls in Goshen, where they live. Pharaoh still does not let them go.

The Egyptians suffer the death of their livestock, boils on the people and the magicians, and the hail. Some of Pharaoh's servants who feared the LORD's word bring their servants and livestock into houses, while those who did not respect it leave them in the field.

The land of Egypt is struck by the livestock pestilence, boils throughout the land, and a hail with lightning worse than any since it became a nation. The hail breaks every tree and every herb of the field. Only Goshen is spared.

Egypt's livestock, including horses, donkeys, camels, herds and flocks, all die on the day the LORD appointed, while none of Israel's livestock die. Livestock left in the field later suffer under the hail, while those brought into houses are sheltered.

l: pestilence on livestock (fifth plague), Exodus, Chapter 9
s: The LORD warns Pharaoh that a very grievous pestilence will strike the livestock in the field and sets the time for the next day. All of Egypt's livestock die, but not one of Israel's. Pharaoh sends to check and finds this true, yet he does not release the people.

Moses sprinkles handfuls of furnace ashes toward the sky before Pharaoh, and they become small dust over Egypt and boils and blisters on man and animal. The magicians cannot stand before Moses because of the boils, which afflict them and all the Egyptians. The LORD then hardens Pharaoh's heart.

The LORD announces a very grievous hail for the next day and urges that livestock and people be brought into shelter or die. It falls with thunder and lightning on all of Egypt, striking people, animals, plants and trees, but not Goshen. It also strikes the flax and barley but not the wheat and spelt, which had not grown up. It ceases when Moses spreads his hands to the LORD.

After the boils the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart and he does not listen. After the hail stops, Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and his servants harden theirs. The chapter closes saying his heart was hardened and he did not let Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.

The LORD tells Moses to go to Pharaoh because he has hardened Pharaoh's heart so that his signs may be shown. Moses and Aaron warn Pharaoh of locusts, and Pharaoh's servants urge him to let the men go; Pharaoh offers to release only the men, and they are driven out. The LORD brings an east wind and locusts devour all remaining greenery in Egypt, Pharaoh confesses sin and asks for forgiveness, and the LORD removes the locusts with a west wind into the Red Sea, then hardens Pharaoh's heart. The LORD then sends a thick darkness over Egypt for three days while Israel has light, and Pharaoh offers to let everyone go except the flocks and herds, which Moses refuses. The LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart again, and Pharaoh orders Moses out, threatening him with death if he sees his face again.

The LORD tells Moses he has hardened Pharaoh's heart and that of his servants so that he may show his signs and so that Israel will tell future generations. He sends the locusts with an east wind, removes them with a west wind into the Red Sea, brings three days of darkness, and hardens Pharaoh's heart twice more.

Moses goes in to Pharaoh with Aaron and warns of locusts, stretches out his rod and later his hand at the LORD's command, and prays to remove the locusts. He refuses Pharaoh's offers to leave the livestock behind, insisting that not a hoof be left. He agrees never to see Pharaoh's face again after being threatened with death.

Aaron accompanies Moses in going to Pharaoh and delivering the LORD's warning about the locusts. He is brought back with Moses to Pharaoh, and is called for again in haste by Pharaoh after the locusts come.

Pharaoh is warned of locusts, offers to let only the men go, and has Moses and Aaron driven out. After the locusts he confesses sin and asks for forgiveness, but his heart is hardened again; after the darkness he offers to let the little ones go but keep the flocks, and finally orders Moses out on pain of death.

Egypt is described by Pharaoh's servants as destroyed, and is covered by locusts that eat everything the hail left, leaving nothing green. It is then covered in thick darkness for three days, and the Egyptians do not see one another or rise from their places.

The children of Israel are the people Moses demands be released to serve the LORD, with young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. During the three days of darkness all of them have light in their dwellings, but Pharaoh does not let them go.

The locusts are brought by an east wind after Moses stretches out his rod, and they spread over all Egypt's borders, darkening the land. They eat every herb and all the fruit of the trees left by the hail, and are then driven into the Red Sea by a strong west wind, leaving none.

The plague of locusts is announced by Moses and Aaron as the result of Pharaoh's refusal, and is described as unparalleled before or after. It prompts Pharaoh to confess sin and ask for its removal, but after it ends the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart and Israel is not released.

The LORD commands Moses to stretch his hand toward the sky to bring a thick darkness that can be felt over Egypt for three days. No one in Egypt sees another or rises from his place, while Israel has light in its dwellings.

The LORD tells Moses that one more plague will fall on Pharaoh and Egypt, after which Pharaoh will drive the Israelites out, and instructs him to have the people ask their neighbors for silver and gold jewels. Moses, who is held in high regard by the Egyptians and Pharaoh's servants, announces to Pharaoh that at midnight the LORD will go through Egypt and kill all the firstborn, from Pharaoh's own to the servant behind the mill, and the livestock's firstborn. A great cry will rise over Egypt, while Israel will be untouched, showing that the LORD distinguishes between Egypt and Israel. Moses leaves Pharaoh in hot anger, and the LORD says Pharaoh will not listen so his wonders may be multiplied. The chapter closes noting that Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart and he did not let Israel go.

The LORD announces one final plague on Egypt and says he will go out into the middle of Egypt at midnight. He gives the people favor with the Egyptians, makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel, and hardens Pharaoh's heart so that his wonders may be multiplied.

Moses receives the LORD's instruction to have the people ask their neighbors for silver and gold jewels, and is described as very great in Egypt in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and the people. He delivers the LORD's warning of the death of the firstborn to Pharaoh and leaves him in hot anger. He and Aaron performed all the wonders before Pharaoh.

Pharaoh is told that his firstborn, who sits on his throne, will die in the coming plague, and that his servants will bow to Moses and urge Israel out. The LORD says he will not listen to Moses, and hardens his heart so that he does not let the Israelites leave.
Egypt is to suffer one more plague, in which the LORD goes into its midst at midnight and all its firstborn die. A great cry, unlike any before or after, will rise throughout the land.

The Egyptians are made favorable toward the people by the LORD, so Israelites may ask them for silver and gold jewels. They are to learn through the plague that the LORD distinguishes between them and Israel, and Pharaoh's servants are foretold to bow to Moses and tell Israel to leave.

The people of Israel are to ask their neighbors for jewels of silver and gold and will be thrust out of Egypt. Not even a dog will bark against them or their animals, showing the LORD's distinction between them and the Egyptians, yet Pharaoh does not let them go.

l: plague of the firstborn, Exodus, Chapter 11
s: The plague of the firstborn is announced as the final plague, coming about midnight when the LORD goes out into the middle of Egypt. It will cause a great cry throughout the land and lead Pharaoh to thrust Israel out altogether.

All the firstborn in Egypt are foretold to die, from Pharaoh's firstborn on the throne to the firstborn of the female servant behind the mill, and all the firstborn of livestock. Israel's people and animals will be spared.

In Exodus 12 the LORD instructs Moses and Aaron in Egypt to establish the Passover: each household is to take a year-old unblemished lamb on the tenth day of the first month, kill it at evening on the fourteenth, put its blood on the door posts and lintel, and eat it roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Moses relays the instructions to the elders, and the LORD strikes all the firstborn of Egypt at midnight while passing over the houses marked with blood. Pharaoh and the Egyptians urge Moses and the Israelites to leave, and the Israelites depart from Rameses to Succoth with unleavened dough, plunder from the Egyptians, and a mixed multitude, after 430 years in Egypt. The chapter also sets out lasting ordinances for the Feast of Unleavened Bread and rules on who may eat the Passover, including circumcision requirements for servants and strangers.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, commands the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and declares he will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt. At midnight he strikes all the firstborn of Egypt, passes over the houses marked with blood, and brings Israel out of Egypt by their armies.

Moses, with Aaron, receives the LORD's instructions for the Passover and relays them to the elders of Israel, telling them to kill the Passover and apply the blood with hyssop. Pharaoh summons him and Aaron by night and tells them to leave Egypt with the Israelites.

Egypt is the land where the LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and where he strikes all the firstborn, so that there is not a house without one dead. It is the land Israel leaves after 430 years, setting out from Rameses.

The children of Israel are commanded to keep the Passover, eat unleavened bread for seven days, and observe these ordinances forever, and they do as the LORD commanded. They plunder the Egyptians, leave Egypt in haste from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot besides children, and are brought out by their armies.

The Egyptians suffer the death of their firstborn, and there is a great cry in Egypt. They urge the Israelites to leave in haste, saying "We are all dead men," and give them silver, gold, and clothing because the LORD gave the people favor in their sight.

Pharaoh's firstborn, who sat on his throne, is among those struck at midnight. Pharaoh rises in the night, calls for Moses and Aaron, and tells them to take the Israelites, their flocks, and their herds and go serve the LORD, asking also for a blessing.

The Passover is established as a memorial feast kept by ordinance forever, named as the LORD's Passover because he passes over the Israelite houses when he strikes Egypt. It is to be eaten in haste, in one house, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and its meaning is to be explained to children; foreigners and hired servants may not eat it, but circumcised servants and strangers may.

Each household takes an unblemished year-old male lamb from the sheep or goats on the tenth day, keeps it until the fourteenth, and kills it at evening. It is roasted whole with its head, legs, and inner parts, none of it left until morning, and none of its bones broken.

l: blood of the lamb (Passover lamb), Exodus, Chapter 12
s: The blood is put on the two door posts and lintel of the houses where the lamb is eaten, applied with a bunch of hyssop from the basin. It serves as a token, so that when the LORD sees it he passes over the house and does not let the destroyer enter.

l: Feast of Unleavened Bread, Exodus, Chapter 12
s: The feast lasts seven days, with no yeast in the houses and holy convocations on the first and seventh days, with no work except preparing food. Anyone who eats leavened bread in that time is to be cut off from Israel, and the feast is to be kept forever because the LORD brought Israel's armies out on that day.

At midnight the LORD strikes all the firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh's firstborn on the throne to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon, and the firstborn of livestock. Their deaths leave no house in Egypt without one dead.

After the striking of the firstborn, Israel is thrust out in haste, taking unprepared dough, plunder, flocks, herds, and a mixed multitude from Rameses to Succoth. It occurs at the end of 430 years, to the day, and is called a night to be much observed to the LORD throughout their generations.

In Exodus 13 the LORD tells Moses to sanctify all firstborn of the children of Israel, man and animal, as his own. Moses instructs the people to remember the day they left Egypt, to eat unleavened bread for seven days with a feast on the seventh, and to tell their sons why, once they are in the land of the Canaanite and other peoples. Moses also gives rules for the firstborn: males of animals are the LORD's, a donkey's firstborn is redeemed with a lamb or has its neck broken, and human firstborn sons are redeemed, in memory of the LORD killing Egypt's firstborn after Pharaoh refused to let Israel go. After Pharaoh releases the people, God leads them by the wilderness road by the Red Sea rather than the Philistine road so they will not turn back at the sight of war, and Moses carries Joseph's bones. They camp at Etham, and the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

The LORD claims all firstborn of man and animal as his and commands the observances of unleavened bread and firstborn redemption as memorials of bringing Israel out of Egypt by strength of hand. He killed all the firstborn in Egypt after Pharaoh refused to let the people go. God then leads Israel by the wilderness route rather than the Philistine road, and the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

Moses receives the LORD's command to sanctify the firstborn and relays it to the people along with the instructions about unleavened bread, teaching their sons, and redeeming firstborn. He takes the bones of Joseph with him, fulfilling the oath Joseph had made the children of Israel swear.

The children of Israel are told to remember the day they left Egypt, keep seven days of unleavened bread, and redeem their firstborn sons and donkeys once in the promised land. They go up armed out of Egypt, are led by the wilderness road by the Red Sea, and encamp at Etham after journeying from Succoth.

Egypt is described as the house of bondage from which the LORD brought Israel out by strength of hand. The LORD killed all its firstborn, of man and of livestock, after Pharaoh stubbornly refused to release the people.

The LORD claims all firstborn that open the womb, of man and animal, as his, and the males are to be set apart to him. Firstborn donkeys are redeemed with a lamb or have their necks broken, and human firstborn sons are redeemed, in memory of the LORD killing Egypt's firstborn.

l: Feast of Unleavened Bread, Exodus, Chapter 13
s: Unleavened bread is to be eaten for seven days in the month Abib, with no leavened bread or yeast seen within Israel's borders and a feast to the LORD on the seventh day. It is to be kept yearly in the land and explained to sons as being because of what the LORD did when Israel left Egypt.
The pillar of cloud is the form in which the LORD goes before Israel by day to lead them on their way. It does not depart from before the people.
The pillar of fire is the form in which the LORD goes before Israel by night to give them light so they can travel day and night. It does not depart from before the people.

The departure from Egypt is to be remembered as the day the LORD brought Israel out of the house of bondage by a strong hand, and it is marked by signs on the hand and between the eyes. After Pharaoh let the people go, God avoided the Philistine road and led them around by the wilderness, and they traveled from Succoth to Etham.

The LORD instructs Moses to have the children of Israel turn back and encamp by the sea before Pihahiroth, saying he will harden Pharaoh's heart so that Pharaoh pursues them and the LORD gains honor over him. Pharaoh and his servants regret letting Israel go and chase them with six hundred chosen chariots and all the chariots of Egypt, overtaking the Israelites by the sea. The frightened Israelites complain to Moses, who tells them to stand still and see the LORD's salvation. At the LORD's command Moses stretches out his hand, a strong east wind divides the sea, and Israel crosses on dry ground while the pillar of cloud stands between them and the Egyptians. The Egyptians follow into the sea, the LORD confuses them and removes their chariot wheels, and when Moses stretches out his hand again the waters return and drown Pharaoh's entire army, after which Israel fears and believes in the LORD and in Moses.

The LORD directs Moses to have Israel encamp by the sea, hardens the hearts of Pharaoh and the Egyptians so they pursue, and declares he will gain honor over Pharaoh and his armies. He divides the sea with a strong east wind, confuses the Egyptian army and takes off their chariot wheels, then has the waters return and overthrow them. As a result Israel fears and believes in him.

Moses is told by the LORD where Israel should encamp and answers the people's fearful complaints by telling them not to be afraid and to stand still and see the LORD's salvation. At the LORD's command he stretches out his hand over the sea twice, first to divide it and then to make the waters return. At the end the people believe in the LORD and in his servant Moses.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is told the people have fled, and he and his servants change their minds and regret letting Israel go. His heart is hardened by the LORD, and he prepares his chariot, takes his army, and pursues Israel to the sea. He and his chariots, horses, and horsemen are overthrown there, with the LORD gaining honor over him.

The children of Israel obey the instruction to turn back and encamp by the sea, then become very afraid when the Egyptians approach, cry out to the LORD, and complain to Moses that it would have been better to serve the Egyptians. Told to stand still, they walk through the middle of the sea on dry ground with the waters as a wall on their right and left. They see the Egyptians dead on the shore and come to fear and believe in the LORD and Moses.

The Egyptians pursue Israel after the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart and overtake them encamped by the sea. They follow Israel into the middle of the sea, are confused, and say the LORD fights for Israel against them. The returning waters cover them, and Israel sees them dead on the seashore.

Pharaoh's army, including six hundred chosen chariots, all the chariots of Egypt, horsemen, and captains, pursues Israel and overtakes them by the sea. In the sea the LORD confuses the army and takes off the chariot wheels, so they flee. The waters return and cover the chariots and horsemen so that not one of them remains.

The sea lies before Israel's camp at Pihahiroth, between Migdol and Baal Zephon. A strong east wind drives it back all night to make dry land, with waters standing as walls on either side, and it returns to its strength in the morning when Moses stretches out his hand. It covers Pharaoh's army and none of them remain.

The pillar of cloud, with the angel of God, moves from before Israel's camp to stand behind them, coming between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. It is cloud and darkness yet gives light by night, so that neither camp comes near the other all night. In the morning watch the LORD looks out through the pillar of fire and cloud on the Egyptian army and confuses it.

l: parting of the sea, Exodus, Chapter 14
s: At the LORD's command Moses stretches his hand over the sea, and the LORD causes it to go back by a strong east wind all night, making dry land with the waters divided. Israel crosses in the middle of the sea with a wall of water on the right and left. The Egyptians follow, and when Moses stretches out his hand again the waters return and drown them.

Moses and the children of Israel sing a song to the LORD celebrating his triumph in drowning Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and army in the Red Sea, and anticipating that he will bring his people to his holy dwelling while the nations of Philistia, Edom, Moab, and Canaan tremble. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with tambourines and dances, repeating the song's opening line. Moses then leads Israel from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur, where after three days without water they reach Marah, whose waters are bitter. The people murmur, Moses cries to the LORD, and the LORD shows him a tree that sweetens the water when thrown in. There the LORD sets a statute and ordinance, promises healing and freedom from Egypt's diseases in return for obedience, and Israel then camps at Elim with twelve springs and seventy palm trees.

The LORD is praised in the song as a man of war, glorious in power, who overthrew the enemy, led his redeemed people in loving kindness, and will reign forever. He sweetens Marah's bitter waters by showing Moses a tree, tests the people there, and declares himself the LORD who heals them if they obey him.

Moses sings the victory song to the LORD with the children of Israel. He leads Israel from the Red Sea into the wilderness, cries to the LORD when the people murmur at Marah, throws the tree into the water to make it sweet, and delivers the statute, ordinance, and the LORD's promise of healing.

The children of Israel sing with Moses and walk on dry land through the middle of the sea. In the wilderness they find no water for three days, murmur against Moses at Marah, are tested by the LORD, and then encamp at Elim by twelve springs and seventy palm trees.
Pharaoh's chariots and army are cast into the sea, and his horses go in with his chariots and horsemen. The song reports that his chosen captains are sunk in the Red Sea.

The Egyptian army, including Pharaoh's horses, chariots, horsemen, and chosen captains, is overwhelmed when the LORD brings the sea waters back on them. They sink like a stone and like lead in the mighty waters. The song depicts their intent to pursue, overtake, and divide plunder as defeated.

The Red Sea is where Pharaoh's army is drowned, its waters piled up like a heap by the blast of the LORD's nostrils so that Israel walks through on dry land. The waters then return over the Egyptians. Moses afterwards leads Israel onward from it.

Miriam is identified as a prophetess and the sister of Aaron. She takes a tambourine, leads all the women out with tambourines and dances, and answers them by repeating the song's opening praise of the LORD's triumph.

The song is sung by Moses and the children of Israel to the LORD. It praises his triumph over the horse and rider in the sea, declares him incomparable among the gods, and foretells that he will bring his people to his sanctuary while neighboring peoples tremble. It ends with the declaration that the LORD will reign forever and ever, and Miriam repeats its opening line.

Marah is reached after three days in the wilderness without water, and its waters are too bitter to drink, which gives the place its name. The LORD shows Moses a tree that makes the waters sweet, and there he makes a statute and ordinance and tests the people.

The children of Israel arrive in the wilderness of Sin and murmur against Moses and Aaron, wishing they had died in Egypt rather than starve. The LORD promises bread from the sky and meat, and Moses and Aaron tell the people that their murmurings are really against the LORD, whose glory appears in the cloud. Quail cover the camp in the evening, and in the morning the people find manna, which they gather by the omer according to their eating; leftovers spoil except on the sixth day, when a double portion is gathered. The LORD establishes the Sabbath rest on the seventh day, when no manna is found, and Aaron lays up an omer of manna before the Testimony. The Israelites eat manna for forty years until they reach the borders of Canaan.

The LORD hears Israel's murmurings and promises to rain bread from the sky to test whether they will walk in his law. He sends quail in the evening and manna in the morning, appears in glory in the cloud, and gives the Sabbath, rebuking those who go out to gather on the seventh day. He commands that an omer of manna be kept throughout the generations.

Moses tells the people that their murmurings are against the LORD, not against himself and Aaron, and relays the LORD's instructions about gathering an omer per person and keeping nothing until morning. He becomes angry when some leave manna overnight, explains the Sabbath rule when the rulers report the double portion, and commands Aaron to lay up a pot of manna.

Aaron is addressed together with Moses by the murmuring people, and is told by Moses to call the congregation to come close to the LORD. While he speaks, the LORD's glory appears in the cloud. He later takes a pot with an omer-full of manna and lays it up before the Testimony, as the LORD commanded Moses.

The children of Israel reach the wilderness of Sin and murmur against Moses and Aaron, longing for the meat pots of Egypt. They gather manna each according to his eating, with some disobeying by leaving it overnight or going out on the Sabbath to gather. They rest on the seventh day and eat manna for forty years until they reach the borders of Canaan.

Manna appears on the wilderness surface after the dew as a small round thing like frost, which the people name "Manna"; it is white like coriander seed and tastes like wafers with honey. Each person gathers an omer, leftovers breed worms and turn foul except on the Sabbath eve, and it melts in the heat of the sun. An omer-full is kept before the Testimony for generations, and the people eat it for forty years.

The wilderness of Sin lies between Elim and Sinai, and the congregation arrives there on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt. It is the place where the people murmur about hunger and where the quail and manna are first provided.

The Sabbath is presented as a solemn rest, a holy day to the LORD, on the seventh day. On the sixth day the people gather twice as much manna, which does not spoil when kept, and on the seventh none is found. The LORD tells the people to stay in their places that day, and they rest.

The people murmur against Moses and Aaron over hunger, saying they wish they had died in Egypt. Moses declares the murmurings are really against the LORD, who hears them and responds by promising and then providing meat and bread.

The children of Israel travel from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim at the LORD's command, find no water, and quarrel with Moses, who fears they will stone him. The LORD tells Moses to take the elders and his rod and strike the rock in Horeb, and water comes out; Moses names the place Massah and Meribah. Amalek then attacks Israel at Rephidim, and Joshua fights while Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up the hill. Israel prevails while Moses holds up his hand, so Aaron and Hur support his hands until sunset, and Joshua defeats Amalek with the sword. The LORD orders Moses to write the event in a book and declares he will blot out the memory of Amalek, and Moses builds an altar called The LORD our Banner.

Moses is quarreled with by the people over water, asks the LORD what to do, and strikes the rock with his rod before the elders as commanded. He names the place Massah and Meribah, and during Amalek's attack he stands on the hill with God's rod, with Israel prevailing whenever his hand is raised. He is helped by Aaron and Hur, is told to write the event in a book, builds an altar called "The LORD our Banner," and declares the LORD's sworn war with Amalek.

The LORD commands Israel's journey, instructs Moses to strike the rock where he will stand before him in Horeb, and thereby provides water. He tells Moses to write a memorial and says he will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek, and he is said to have sworn to have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

The children of Israel travel to Rephidim, find no water, and quarrel with and murmur against Moses, testing the LORD by asking whether he is among them. They drink water from the rock, and then fight Amalek, prevailing or not depending on whether Moses' hand is raised, until Joshua defeats Amalek.

Amalek comes and fights with Israel at Rephidim, prevailing whenever Moses lets down his hand. Joshua defeats Amalek and his people with the sword, and the LORD declares he will blot out the memory of Amalek and have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

Joshua is told by Moses to choose men and go out to fight Amalek, and he does as Moses says. He defeats Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword, and the LORD tells Moses to rehearse the memorial of this in Joshua's ears.

Rephidim is where Israel encamps and finds there is no water for the people to drink. It is where the people quarrel with Moses, where the rock provides water, and where Amalek comes and fights with Israel.
The LORD says he will stand on the rock in Horeb before Moses. Moses is told to strike it, and water comes out of it so the people may drink.

There is no water at Rephidim, and the thirsty people blame Moses for bringing them out to die of thirst with their children and livestock. The LORD provides water from the rock Moses strikes, so that the people may drink.

Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, and Joshua leads chosen men against them while Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up the hill. Israel prevails when Moses holds up his hand and Amalek prevails when he lets it down, so Aaron and Hur hold his hands steady until sunset. Joshua defeats Amalek with the edge of the sword.

Lacking water at Rephidim, the people quarrel with Moses, demand water, and accuse him of bringing them out of Egypt to kill them with thirst. Moses asks why they quarrel and test the LORD, cries out to the LORD, and the place is named Massah and Meribah because of the quarreling and testing.

Jethro, priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, hears of what God did for Moses and Israel and brings Moses' wife Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to Moses at the Mountain of God. Moses greets him and recounts the LORD's deliverance of Israel from Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and Jethro rejoices, praises the LORD as greater than all gods, and offers a burnt offering and sacrifices, with Aaron and the elders eating bread with him. The next day Jethro sees Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening and tells him this is not good because the work is too heavy for him. He advises Moses to teach the people God's statutes, to represent them before God, and to appoint able, God-fearing, truthful men as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens who will judge small matters while Moses handles great ones. Moses follows the counsel, appoints such rulers, and sends Jethro on his way back to his own land.

Jethro, priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, hears of what God did for Moses and Israel and brings Zipporah and her two sons to Moses at the Mountain of God. He rejoices, declares the LORD greater than all gods, offers a burnt offering and sacrifices, and then advises Moses to share the burden of judging. After Moses follows his advice, he departs for his own land.

Moses meets Jethro with a bow and a kiss, and tells him all the LORD did to Pharaoh and the Egyptians and for Israel on the way. He sits alone judging the people from morning to evening until Jethro rebukes him, then he listens, chooses able men as rulers over the people, and lets Jethro depart.

The LORD is credited with bringing Israel out of Egypt and delivering them from the hand of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and with helping them through hardships on the way. Jethro blesses him and says he now knows the LORD is greater than all gods because of how the Egyptians treated people arrogantly.

Israel is described as the people the LORD delivered out of Egypt, and Moses recounts to Jethro the hardships that came upon them on the way. Aaron and the elders of Israel eat bread with Jethro before God, and Moses chooses able men out of all Israel to be heads over the people.

The people stand around Moses from morning to evening as he judges, coming to him to inquire of God and to have matters settled between a man and his neighbor. After the reorganization they are judged by appointed rulers at all times, and Jethro says they will go to their place in peace.

l: judges and rulers (appointed by Moses), Exodus, Chapter 18
s: Moses chooses able men out of all Israel and makes them heads over the people as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. They judge the people at all times, bringing the hard cases to Moses while judging every small matter themselves.

Moses sits to judge the people from morning to evening, teaching them God's statutes and laws as they bring him their matters. Jethro calls this too heavy for one man, and the work is restructured so that rulers judge small matters and only hard or great cases go to Moses.

l: Jethro's counsel on delegating judgment, Exodus, Chapter 18
s: Jethro tells Moses that he and the people will wear out if he judges alone. He advises Moses to represent the people before God, teach them the statutes and laws, and appoint able, God-fearing men of truth who hate unjust gain as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Moses listens and does all that Jethro said.

In the third month after leaving Egypt, the children of Israel arrive at the wilderness of Sinai and camp before the mountain. The LORD calls to Moses from the mountain and offers Israel the status of his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, if they obey his voice and keep his covenant. The people answer together that they will do all the LORD has spoken, and the LORD instructs Moses to sanctify them, set bounds around the mountain, and prepare for the third day. On that day thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a loud trumpet, fire, and smoke and quaking mark the LORD's descent on Mount Sinai, and Moses goes up at his call. The LORD then sends Moses back down to warn the people and priests not to break through to gaze, and Moses goes down to tell them.

The LORD calls to Moses from Mount Sinai and tells him to remind Israel of what he did to the Egyptians and how he bore them on eagles' wings. He offers them a covenant making them his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and commands sanctification and boundaries before he comes down. On the third day he descends on the mountain in fire, answers Moses by a voice, calls him to the top, and twice warns that the people and priests must not break through lest he break out on them.

Moses goes up to God, receives the LORD's words for Israel, and reports them to the elders and then the people. He carries the people's answer back to the LORD, sanctifies the people, instructs them to be ready by the third day and abstain from sexual relations, and leads them out to meet God. He speaks and is answered by God, climbs to the top of Mount Sinai when called, objects that the bounds are already set, and is sent down again to warn the people, returning later with Aaron.

The children of Israel come to the wilderness of Sinai from Rephidim and camp before the mountain. They answer together that they will do all the LORD has spoken, then wash their garments and prepare for three days. On the third day they tremble at the thunder, lightning and trumpet, stand at the lower part of the mountain, and are forbidden on pain of death to touch it or break through to the LORD.

Mount Sinai is where Israel camps and where the LORD calls to Moses. It is to have bounds set around it, and anyone who touches it, man or animal, is to be put to death. On the third day it is covered by a thick cloud, smokes like a furnace, and quakes greatly as the LORD descends on it in fire, and Moses is called to its top.

l: covenant (between the LORD and Israel), Exodus, Chapter 19
s: The LORD conditions Israel's special standing on obeying his voice and keeping his covenant: they will be his own possession from among all peoples, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people respond together that all the LORD has spoken they will do. This unit records the offer and acceptance but not its terms.

The LORD announces he will come to Moses in a thick cloud so the people may hear him speak and believe Moses forever, and that he will come down in the sight of all the people on the third day. On that morning thunders, lightnings, a thick cloud, an exceedingly loud trumpet, fire, smoke and a quaking mountain accompany his descent, and the people tremble. God answers Moses by a voice, and strict bounds and warnings keep the people and priests from breaking through to gaze.

God speaks the commandments to the people, identifying himself as the LORD who brought them out of Egypt. He forbids other gods, idols, misuse of his name, and murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and coveting, and commands keeping the Sabbath holy and honoring parents. The people, terrified by thunder, lightning, trumpet sound, and smoke on the mountain, stay at a distance and ask Moses to speak with God for them. Moses reassures them that God has come to test them, then approaches the thick darkness where God is. The LORD then instructs Moses to tell Israel not to make gods of silver or gold and gives rules for building an altar of earth or uncut stone, without steps.

The LORD speaks all the commandments, identifying himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt and as a jealous God who visits iniquity on those who hate him and shows loving kindness to thousands who love him. He then tells Moses what to say to Israel about not making gods of silver or gold and about how to build his altar, promising to come and bless them where he records his name.

Moses is asked by the frightened people to speak with God on their behalf, and he reassures them that God has come to test them so that his fear will keep them from sin. He draws near to the thick darkness where God is and receives the LORD's instructions to relay to the children of Israel.

The people are addressed with the commandments and perceive the thunderings, lightnings, trumpet sound, and smoking mountain, which makes them tremble and stay at a distance. They ask Moses to speak with them instead of God, fearing they will die, and are told they have seen that God talked with them from heaven.

The commandments are spoken by God and include: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the LORD's name, remembering the Sabbath, honoring father and mother, and prohibitions on murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony, and coveting. They cover duties toward God and toward neighbors, and some carry stated consequences or promises, such as long days in the land for honoring parents.

God forbids making an idol or any image of anything in the heavens, on the earth, or in the water, and forbids bowing to or serving them. Later he specifically forbids making gods of silver or gold to be alongside him.

The Sabbath is commanded to be remembered and kept holy: six days for labor, and the seventh a Sabbath to the LORD on which no one in the household, including servants, livestock, and the stranger within the gates, may work. The reason given is that the LORD made heaven, earth, and sea in six days, rested on the seventh, blessed it, and made it holy.

The LORD instructs that his altar be made of earth for burnt offerings and peace offerings of sheep and cattle, or of uncut stone, since using a tool on the stones pollutes it. It must not be approached by steps, so that nakedness is not exposed on it.

Chapter 21 opens a set of ordinances to be set before the people, beginning with rules for Hebrew servants, who serve six years and go free in the seventh, and for a daughter sold as a female servant, who is protected from being sold abroad and must receive food, clothing and marital rights. It then lists laws on violence: death for murder, attacking or cursing parents, and kidnapping, with provision of a place of refuge for unintentional killing, and compensation for non-fatal injuries. Masters who injure servants face punishment or must free them for a lost eye or tooth, while a pregnant woman harmed in a fight brings a fine or, if further harm follows, life for life, eye for eye and so on. The chapter closes with rules on liability for a goring bull, an owner's responsibility when he knew of the habit, an uncovered pit, and one bull killing another.

A bought Hebrew servant serves six years and goes out free in the seventh without payment, taking his wife if he came married. If his master gave him a wife, she and her children stay with the master. A servant who declares love for his master, wife and children has his ear bored with an awl at the door or doorpost and serves forever.

l: master (of the Hebrew servant), Exodus, Chapter 21
s: The master must free the Hebrew servant in the seventh year, but keeps a wife he gave the servant and her children. If the servant refuses to leave, the master brings him to God and the door and bores his ear with an awl. A master who has married a female servant and is displeased with her must let her be redeemed and may not sell her to a foreign people.

l: daughter (sold as female servant), Exodus, Chapter 21
s: A daughter sold as a female servant does not go out as male servants do. If her master is displeased with her, she is to be redeemed and cannot be sold to a foreign people; if married to his son she is treated as a daughter. If denied food, clothing or marital rights she may go free without paying.
The chapter begins by introducing the ordinances that are to be set before the people. They cover servants, homicide and injury, retaliation, and liability for animals and pits.

l: servitude and release of servants, Exodus, Chapter 21
s: Servitude terms are limited: Hebrew male servants go free in the seventh year, and female servants have protections regarding redemption and support. Injuring a servant's eye or tooth requires the master to free the servant. The permanent-service ear-boring rite is the exception for a servant who chooses to stay.

Striking a man dead brings death, except for unintentional killing, where a place of flight is appointed, while a scheming killer is taken even from the altar. Attacking or cursing parents and kidnapping are also capital offenses. Non-fatal fights require payment for lost time and healing, and a master who kills a servant under his hand is punished, though not if the servant survives a day or two.

l: male servant and maid, Exodus, Chapter 21
s: A servant or maid struck with a rod who dies under the master's hand means the master is punished, but no punishment follows if the servant gets up after a day or two, since the servant is his property. If the master destroys a servant's or maid's eye or tooth, the servant goes free. If a bull gores a servant, thirty shekels of silver go to the master and the ox is stoned.

l: lex talionis (eye for eye), Exodus, Chapter 21
s: If harm follows when a pregnant woman is hurt in a fight, life is taken for life. The text lists eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound and bruise for bruise.

A bull that gores a man or woman to death is stoned and its meat is not eaten. If it was known to gore before, the bull is stoned and its owner is also put to death. A bull that kills another's bull leads to selling the live one and dividing the price and the carcass.

l: owner of the bull, Exodus, Chapter 21
s: An owner is not held responsible when his bull gores someone to death without prior habit. If the bull had a known habit and he did not keep it in, he is put to death, though a ransom may be imposed for his life. He must pay bull for bull and keep the dead animal if his habitually goring bull kills another's.

l: liability for animals and property, Exodus, Chapter 21
s: A man who opens or digs an uncovered pit must make good the loss when a bull or donkey falls in, paying the owner and keeping the dead animal. When one man's bull kills another's, the live bull and the carcass are divided, unless the bull was known to gore, in which case its owner pays bull for bull. A bull killing a servant requires thirty shekels to the master.

Chapter 22 sets out laws on theft, property damage, and entrusted goods. A thief who steals an ox or sheep and kills or sells it pays five oxen or four sheep, while one found with the live animal pays double. Owners of animals or fires that damage another's field must make restitution, and disputes over goods kept by a neighbor are settled before God by oath or judgment. The chapter then turns to sexual and religious offenses, including seduction of a virgin, sorcery, bestiality, and sacrifice to other gods. It ends with commands to protect aliens, widows, fatherless children, and the poor, to honor God and rulers, to give firstfruits and firstborn to the LORD, and to avoid eating torn meat.

The LORD is the one before whom disputes over goods are brought, and his oath settles cases between neighbors. He commands that no sacrifice be made to any other god and that firstfruits, firstborn sons, and firstborn livestock be given to him. He promises to hear the cry of the oppressed, including widows, fatherless children, and the poor, and says his wrath will kill those who exploit them, because he is gracious.

A thief who kills or sells a stolen ox or sheep pays five oxen or four sheep, and one found with the live animal pays double. A thief killed while breaking in at night incurs no bloodshed guilt for the killer, but after sunrise the killer is guilty. A thief who cannot make restitution is to be sold for his theft.
The alien is not to be wronged or oppressed. The reason given is that the people were themselves aliens in the land of Egypt.

l: widow and fatherless child, Exodus, Chapter 22
s: Widows and fatherless children must not be taken advantage of. If they cry out to the LORD, he will hear and respond with wrath, killing the oppressors with the sword so that their own wives become widows and their children fatherless.

A neighbor may entrust money, goods, or animals to another to keep, and the keeper's responsibility depends on the circumstances. If goods are stolen and the thief is found, the thief pays double; if not, the keeper comes before God to determine whether he took them. A borrower must make good an injured or dead animal unless its owner was with it, and a keeper who swears by the LORD that he did not take an animal that died, was injured, or was driven away unseen is not required to make restitution.

l: stolen animals and livestock, Exodus, Chapter 22
s: Oxen, sheep, and donkeys are the main stolen property in these laws, with penalties of fivefold, fourfold, or double depending on whether they were killed or sold or found alive. Animals that are lost, injured, or die while kept by a neighbor are handled by oath or restitution. Animals torn by wild beasts need not be replaced if the torn carcass is brought as evidence, but the meat of such animals must not be eaten and is cast to the dogs. Firstborn livestock stay with the mother seven days and are given to the LORD on the eighth.

l: theft and restitution laws, Exodus, Chapter 22
s: The chapter fixes restitution for theft, for animals that graze in another's field, for fires that spread, and for goods lost while kept or borrowed by a neighbor. Penalties range from double to five times the value, and disputes are brought before God. The laws also cover seduction of a virgin, who must be given a dowry and married or paid for, and forbid charging interest to the poor and keeping a pledged garment overnight.

In Exodus 23, God gives the Israelites laws on honest testimony and impartial justice, including bans on false reports, following a crowd to pervert justice, bribes, and oppressing aliens, along with a duty to return an enemy's stray animal and help his fallen donkey. He then sets a sabbatical year of rest for the land and a weekly Sabbath rest, and requires three annual feasts: unleavened bread, harvest, and ingathering. God promises to send an angel before the people to bring them into the land and to drive out the Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Canaanite, Hivite, and Jebusite little by little. He forbids serving or covenanting with their gods and promises blessing, health, and a border from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines if the Israelites obey.

The LORD gives the Israelites laws on justice, rest, and worship, and calls for three annual feasts before him. He promises to send an angel, to be an enemy to Israel's enemies, to drive out the land's inhabitants little by little, and to bless and heal the people if they serve him.

The Israelites are commanded to give honest testimony, treat the poor, enemies, and aliens fairly, keep the sabbatical year and Sabbath, and observe three feasts. They are told to obey the angel, avoid other gods, and make no covenant with the land's inhabitants, and are promised a border from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines.

The angel is sent before the Israelites to keep them on the way and bring them to the prepared place, and to bring them in to the peoples of the land. The people must listen to his voice and not provoke him, since he will not pardon disobedience and God's name is in him.

l: inhabitants of the land (Canaan), Exodus, Chapter 23
s: The Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Canaanite, Hivite, and Jebusite are to be cut off, with the hornet and God's terror driving them out gradually so the land does not become desolate. The Israelites must make no covenant with them and not let them dwell in the land, lest they become a snare.

l: gods of the inhabitants, Exodus, Chapter 23
s: The Israelites are told not to invoke the names of other gods, bow down to them, serve them, or make a covenant with them. Their pillars are to be demolished, and serving them would be a snare.

l: justice and fair testimony laws, Exodus, Chapter 23
s: These laws forbid spreading false reports, joining the wicked as a malicious witness, following a crowd to pervert justice, and taking bribes. They also forbid favoring a poor man in his cause, denying justice to the poor, and killing the innocent, and require returning an enemy's strayed ox or donkey and helping his fallen donkey. Aliens must not be oppressed, since the Israelites were aliens in Egypt.

The land is to be sown and harvested for six years and left to rest and lie fallow in the seventh. The poor of the people eat what grows, and animals of the field eat what they leave. The same applies to vineyards and olive groves.
The Israelites work six days and rest on the seventh. This lets their ox and donkey rest, and the servant's son and the alien be refreshed.

l: Feast of Unleavened Bread, Exodus, Chapter 23
s: The Israelites are to eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month Abib, because they came out of Egypt in it. No one is to appear before God empty-handed.
The feast of harvest is the feast of the first fruits of the Israelites' labors, which they sow in the field. It is one of three yearly feasts at which all males appear before the Lord GOD.
The feast of ingathering is held at the end of the year, when the Israelites gather in their labors from the field. It is one of three yearly feasts at which all males appear before the Lord GOD.

The LORD tells Moses to come up with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to worship from a distance, while Moses alone may come near. Moses relays the LORD's words and ordinances, and the people promise to do all that the LORD has said. Moses writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars, has young men offer burnt and peace offerings, reads the book of the covenant to the people, and sprinkles them with blood, declaring it the blood of the covenant. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders then go up and see the God of Israel, and they eat and drink. Moses goes further up Mount Sinai with Joshua, leaving Aaron and Hur in charge of disputes, and stays in the cloud of the LORD's glory for forty days and forty nights.

The LORD instructs Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to worship from a distance, with Moses alone permitted to come near. He is seen by Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the elders, who are not harmed, and he promises Moses stone tablets with the law and commands. His glory settles on Mount Sinai in a cloud and appears like devouring fire, and on the seventh day he calls to Moses from the cloud.

Moses relays the LORD's words to the people, writes them down, builds an altar with twelve pillars, reads the book of the covenant aloud, and sprinkles the people with blood. He goes up the mountain with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the elders, then goes higher with Joshua, his servant, and enters the cloud. He remains on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

Aaron is told to come up and worship from a distance with Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders, and he goes up and sees the God of Israel. Moses then leaves him and Hur with the elders so that anyone in a dispute can go to them.

l: elders (of the people of Israel), Exodus, Chapter 24
s: The seventy elders are told to worship from a distance and later go up with Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu. They see the God of Israel, are not harmed, and eat and drink. Moses tells them to wait for his return, with Aaron and Hur available to settle disputes.

The people hear Moses relay the LORD's words and ordinances and answer with one voice that they will do all that he has spoken. After the book of the covenant is read, they promise to do it and be obedient, and Moses sprinkles them with blood. They are not to go up the mountain, and they see the LORD's glory as devouring fire on its top.

At the base of the mountain Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars. The LORD's glory settles on Mount Sinai, and a cloud covers it for six days. Moses goes up into the cloud and stays there forty days and forty nights.

l: book of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 24
s: Moses writes all the LORD's words and takes this book to read in the hearing of the people. After hearing it, the people say they will do all that the LORD has said and be obedient.

l: blood of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 24
s: Moses puts half of the blood from the peace offerings in basins and sprinkles half on the altar. He then sprinkles the blood on the people and declares it the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with them concerning all these words.

l: covenant (between the LORD and Israel), Exodus, Chapter 24
s: The covenant is established as the people twice promise to obey the LORD's words, the book of the covenant is read, and the offerings are made. It is sealed when Moses sprinkles the people with blood, calling it the blood of the covenant the LORD has made with them concerning all these words.

The LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel to bring a freewill offering of materials such as gold, silver, bronze, fabrics, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, and stones, so they can make a sanctuary where he may dwell among them. He then gives detailed specifications for the furnishings: an acacia-wood ark overlaid with gold and carried by poles, a gold mercy seat with two hammered-gold cherubim, a gold-overlaid table for the bread of the presence, and a hammered pure-gold lamp stand with six branches and seven lamps. The LORD says he will meet with Moses and speak from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim. Everything must follow the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain.

The LORD speaks to Moses and commands that an offering be taken so a sanctuary can be made for him to dwell among the people. He gives exact patterns for the ark, mercy seat, table, and lamp stand, and promises to meet with Moses and speak from above the mercy seat between the cherubim.

Moses is told to speak to the children of Israel about taking an offering for the LORD. He is the one to whom the LORD will speak from above the mercy seat, and he is reminded to see that everything is made after the pattern shown to him on the mountain.

The children of Israel are to bring an offering for the LORD, taken from everyone whose heart makes him willing. They are to make the sanctuary and its furnishings, and the LORD will give commands for them from the mercy seat.

l: offering (for the tabernacle work), Exodus, Chapter 25
s: The offering is to be taken from everyone whose heart makes him willing. It consists of gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats' hair, rams' skins dyed red, sea cow hides, acacia wood, oil for the light, spices for the anointing oil and sweet incense, onyx stones, and stones for the ephod and breastplate.
The LORD commands the people to make him a sanctuary so that he may dwell among them. It and all its furniture must be made according to the pattern of the tabernacle that he shows Moses.

l: ark of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 25
s: The ark is to be made of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high, overlaid inside and outside with pure gold with a gold molding. It has four gold rings in its feet and acacia poles overlaid with gold, which must stay in the rings, and the covenant the LORD will give is to be put inside it.

The mercy seat is to be made of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide, and placed on top of the ark. The LORD says he will meet with Moses there and speak from above it, between the two cherubim.

l: cherubim (on the mercy seat), Exodus, Chapter 25
s: Two cherubim of hammered gold are to be made of one piece with the mercy seat, one at each end. They spread their wings upward, covering the mercy seat, with their faces toward one another and toward the mercy seat.

The table is to be made of acacia wood, two cubits long, a cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high, overlaid with pure gold and given a gold molding and a hand-width rim. It has four gold rings and gold-overlaid acacia poles for carrying, pure gold dishes, spoons, ladles, and bowls, and the bread of the presence is to be set on it before the LORD always.

The lamp stand is to be made of pure gold in hammered work, with base, shaft, cups, buds, and flowers all of one piece. It has six branches, three on each side, with almond-blossom cups, seven lamps to give light in front of it, and pure gold snuffers and snuff dishes, all made from a talent of pure gold.

Chapter 26 gives instructions for constructing the tabernacle. Ten curtains of fine twined linen with blue, purple, scarlet and cherubim are coupled in two sets of five by fifty blue loops and fifty gold clasps, and eleven goats' hair curtains are coupled with bronze clasps to cover the tent, with coverings of rams' skins dyed red and sea cow hides above. The framework is made of upright acacia boards (twenty on the south, twenty on the north, eight on the west) set in silver sockets and held by gold-overlaid acacia bars. A veil of blue, purple, scarlet and linen hung on four gold-overlaid pillars separates the holy place from the most holy, where the ark of the covenant and mercy seat are placed. The table and lamp stand are set outside the veil, and a screen with five pillars on bronze sockets is made for the door of the Tent.

The tabernacle is to be made of ten linen curtains with cherubim, coupled into a single unit by gold clasps, and is to be set up according to the pattern shown on the mountain. It is covered by goats' hair curtains, rams' skins and sea cow hides, and is divided by a veil into the holy place and the most holy place.

l: curtains of fine twined linen (tabernacle's ten curtains), Exodus, Chapter 26
s: Ten curtains of fine twined linen, blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubim, are to be made by a skillful workman, each twenty-eight cubits long and four wide. They are joined in two sets of five using fifty blue loops and fifty gold clasps so that the tabernacle is a unit.

l: curtains of goats' hair (covering over the tabernacle), Exodus, Chapter 26
s: Eleven goats' hair curtains, each thirty cubits long and four wide, are to be made as a covering over the tabernacle. They are coupled in sets of five and six with fifty loops and fifty bronze clasps, the sixth is doubled over at the front of the tent, and the overhang hangs over the back and sides. Coverings of rams' skins dyed red and sea cow hides go above them.

Upright acacia boards, each ten cubits long and one and a half wide with two tenons, form the walls: twenty on the south, twenty on the north, and eight on the west including two corner boards. Each rests on two silver sockets (forty per long side, sixteen on the west), is overlaid with gold with gold rings, and is held by acacia bars, five per side, the middle bar passing through end to end.

The veil is to be made of blue, purple, scarlet and fine twined linen with cherubim, the work of a skillful workman. It hangs under the clasps on four gold-overlaid acacia pillars with gold hooks on silver sockets, and separates the holy place from the most holy.

l: ark of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 26
s: The ark of the covenant is to be brought in within the veil, into the most holy place. The mercy seat is to be put on top of it there.

This chapter gives instructions for making the altar of acacia wood, which is square, five cubits by five cubits and three cubits high, with horns of one piece with it, overlaid with bronze. It lists the bronze vessels, a bronze grating with four rings, and the acacia poles overlaid with bronze for carrying it, and says it is to be made hollow with planks as shown on the mountain. It then specifies the court of the tabernacle: hangings of fine twined linen on the south, north, west and east sides, with pillars set in bronze sockets, silver hooks and fillets, and a twenty-cubit embroidered screen for the gate. Finally, the children of Israel are commanded to bring pure olive oil beaten for the light so a lamp burns continually, and Aaron and his sons are to keep it in order in the Tent of Meeting from evening to morning before the LORD as a statute forever.

The altar is to be made of acacia wood, square, five cubits long and wide and three cubits high, with horns of one piece with it, overlaid with bronze. It is to have bronze vessels (pots, shovels, basins, meat hooks, fire pans), a bronze network grating with four rings, and acacia poles overlaid with bronze for carrying, and it is to be made hollow with planks as shown on the mountain.

The court is to be one hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and five cubits high, enclosed by fine twined linen hangings on pillars set in bronze sockets. Its pillars have silver hooks and fillets, its pins are bronze, and its gate is a twenty-cubit screen of blue, purple, scarlet and fine twined linen.

l: hangings (court of the tabernacle), Exodus, Chapter 27
s: The hangings are of fine twined linen: one hundred cubits on each of the south and north sides (twenty pillars and sockets each), fifty cubits on the west side (ten pillars and sockets), and on the east side fifty cubits in total, with fifteen cubits on each side of the gate (three pillars and sockets each). The pillars have silver hooks and fillets and bronze sockets.
Pure olive oil, beaten for the light, is to be brought by the children of Israel so that a lamp may burn continually.

Aaron, with his sons, is assigned to keep the lamp in order in the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil before the covenant, from evening to morning before the LORD. This is a statute forever throughout their generations.
Aaron's sons, together with Aaron, are to keep the lamp in order from evening to morning before the LORD in the Tent of Meeting. This is a statute forever throughout their generations.
The children of Israel are to be commanded to bring pure olive oil beaten for the light so that a lamp burns continually. The lamp's upkeep by Aaron and his sons is a statute forever on their behalf.
The Tent of Meeting is the place where the lamp is kept, outside the veil which is before the covenant. Aaron and his sons keep the lamp in order there from evening to morning before the LORD.

In Exodus 28, the LORD instructs that Aaron, his brother, and Aaron's sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar be set apart from the children of Israel to minister in the priest's office. Wise-hearted workers are to make holy garments for glory and beauty: a breastplate, ephod, robe, fitted tunic, turban, and sash, using gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. The ephod carries two engraved onyx stones with the tribes' names on its shoulders, and the breastplate of judgment holds twelve engraved stones and the Urim and the Thummim over Aaron's heart. The robe has pomegranates and golden bells, and a gold plate engraved 'HOLY TO THE LORD' is worn on Aaron's forehead. Aaron's sons receive tunics, sashes, headbands, and linen pants, and all are to be anointed, consecrated, and sanctified, with the pants worn so they do not bear iniquity and die.

Aaron is called, with his sons, to minister to the LORD in the priest's office and is to be clothed in holy garments made for glory and beauty. He bears the names of the children of Israel on his shoulders and on his heart as a memorial, carries the judgment of Israel before the LORD continually, and wears the gold plate on his forehead to bear the iniquity of the holy things so the people are accepted. The bells on his robe must sound when he enters and leaves the holy place so that he does not die.

Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar are named as Aaron's sons who are to minister with him in the priest's office. They are to receive tunics, sashes, and headbands for glory and beauty, and linen pants covering their flesh from waist to thighs. Together with Aaron they are to be anointed, consecrated, and sanctified, and the pants are a statute forever so they do not bear iniquity and die when entering the Tent of Meeting or approaching the altar.

The children of Israel are the group from whom Aaron and his sons are brought near to serve as priests. Their names are engraved in birth order on the two onyx stones on the ephod's shoulders and on the twelve breastplate stones for the twelve tribes. Aaron bears these names and their judgment before the LORD as a memorial, and their holy gifts are made acceptable through the plate on his forehead.

The LORD commands Moses-era instructions in this unit by directing that Aaron and his sons minister to him in the priest's office, and he specifies the garments in detail. He has filled the wise-hearted workers with the spirit of wisdom to make them. He is the one before whom Aaron bears the memorial names, the judgment, and the iniquity of the holy things, and entering his presence requires the prescribed garments lest one die.

l: holy garments (for Aaron and his sons), Exodus, Chapter 28
s: The holy garments are a breastplate, ephod, robe, fitted tunic, turban, and sash for Aaron, made by wise-hearted workers from gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. They sanctify Aaron for ministry and give glory and beauty. Aaron's sons receive tunics, sashes, headbands, and linen pants, and the robe's bells and the forehead plate are added to Aaron's attire.

The ephod is made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen as skillful work, with two shoulder straps and a skillfully woven band of the same piece. Two onyx stones engraved with six tribal names each, set in gold, sit on its shoulder straps as memorial stones, attached with gold settings and braided chains. The breastplate is bound to its rings with a blue lace so it does not swing out, and the robe of the ephod is to be all blue.

The breastplate is made like the ephod's work, square, folded double, and a span in length and width. It holds four rows of three stones set in gold, twelve in all, each engraved with a tribe's name, and the Urim and the Thummim are placed in it. It hangs by gold braided chains and rings, bound to the ephod with a blue lace, and rests on Aaron's heart as a memorial before the LORD continually.

Aaron and his sons are to be clothed in the holy garments, anointed, consecrated, and sanctified so that they may minister to the LORD in the priest's office. The linen pants are required whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar, so that they do not bear iniquity and die. This is stated as a statute forever for Aaron and his offspring.

Chapter 29 gives the LORD's instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests: washing, clothing, and anointing Aaron, then offering a young bull as a sin offering, one ram as a burnt offering, and a second ram of consecration whose blood marks the priests. The priests receive portions of the wave offerings, eat the consecration ram and bread at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and any leftovers are burned. Aaron's holy garments pass to his sons after him, and the seven-day consecration includes daily sin offerings to cleanse and sanctify the altar. The chapter ends with the daily offering of two lambs, morning and evening, with flour, oil, and wine, and the LORD's promise to meet Israel, sanctify the place by his glory, and dwell among the children of Israel as their God.

Aaron is to be washed, clothed in the tunic, robe of the ephod, ephod, breastplate, band, turban, and holy crown, and anointed with oil on his head. He and his sons lay hands on the offerings, receive blood on the right ear, thumb, and toe, and are sprinkled with blood and oil. He is to be consecrated for seven days and will eat the consecration meat and bread with his sons.

Aaron's sons are to be brought, given tunics, belts, and headbands, and consecrated along with Aaron. They lay hands on the offerings, receive blood on the right ear, thumb, and toe, and share the wave offering portions and the consecration meal. They will hold the priesthood by a perpetual statute, and one of them will wear Aaron's garments after him.

The LORD commands the detailed rites that make Aaron and his sons holy to minister as priests. He declares that he will meet the children of Israel at the Tent of Meeting, sanctify the tent, the altar, and the priests, and dwell among Israel as their God, the one who brought them out of Egypt.

The Tent of Meeting is the site where Aaron and his sons are brought and washed, where the bull is killed, and where the consecration meal is eaten at its door. The daily burnt offering is made at its door, where the LORD will meet and speak with Israel. The LORD promises to sanctify it.

The altar receives the bull's blood on its horns and the rams' blood sprinkled around it, and the fat and offerings are burned on it. It is to be cleansed, anointed, and atoned for over seven days until it is most holy, so that whatever touches it is holy. The daily lamb offerings are made on it, and the LORD says he will sanctify it.

l: bull (sin offering for Aaron's consecration), Exodus, Chapter 29
s: A young bull is brought to the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head, and it is killed before the LORD. Its blood is put on the altar's horns and poured at the base, its fat and organs are burned on the altar, and its meat, skin, and dung are burned outside the camp as a sin offering. A bull of sin offering is offered every day of the seven days for atonement.

l: burnt offering ram (first ram of consecration), Exodus, Chapter 29
s: The first ram has hands laid on its head by Aaron and his sons and is killed. Its blood is sprinkled around the altar, and the ram is cut in pieces, with innards and legs washed, and burned whole on the altar as a burnt offering, a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

l: ram of consecration (second ram), Exodus, Chapter 29
s: The second ram has hands laid on it and is killed. Its blood is put on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons and sprinkled on the altar, and with oil on the priests and their garments. Its fat, right thigh, and one loaf, cake, and wafer are waved and burned, its breast is Aaron's portion, and its meat is boiled and eaten by the priests at the tent door, with leftovers burned by morning.

l: holy garments (for Aaron and his sons), Exodus, Chapter 29
s: Aaron's holy garments are the tunic, robe of the ephod, ephod, breastplate, woven band, turban, and holy crown, put on him for consecration. They are to pass to his sons after him, to be anointed and consecrated in them. The son who is priest in his place is to wear them seven days when he enters the Tent of Meeting to minister.

l: consecration of the priests, Exodus, Chapter 29
s: The consecration involves washing, clothing, and anointing, the sin offering bull, the burnt offering ram, and the ram of consecration with blood and oil applied to the priests. It lasts seven days, with daily atonement for the altar, and the meat and bread are eaten only by the priests, not by a stranger.

Aaron and his sons are to hold the priesthood by a perpetual statute. Their portion of the wave offering from the children of Israel is theirs forever, and the priesthood continues through the sons who succeed Aaron in the holy garments.

l: daily continual burnt offering, Exodus, Chapter 29
s: Two year-old lambs are to be offered on the altar every day, one in the morning and one at evening. Each is accompanied by a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine as a drink offering. It is a continual offering throughout the generations at the tent door, where the LORD will meet and speak with Israel.

The children of Israel are to provide the wave offering portions from their peace offerings to Aaron and his sons as their portion forever. The LORD promises to meet them at the Tent of Meeting, sanctify the place by his glory, and dwell among them as their God. They will know he is the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.

Moses is not named in this unit, but the LORD addresses him as "you" throughout. He is told to carry out the consecration of Aaron and his sons: washing, clothing, and anointing them, performing the sacrifices, and applying blood and oil. He is also told to cleanse and anoint the altar and to offer the daily lambs.

In Exodus 30 the LORD gives Moses instructions for further tabernacle furnishings and rites. He describes an acacia-wood altar of incense overlaid with gold, on which Aaron is to burn incense every morning and evening. He sets a half-shekel atonement ransom for each Israelite counted in a census, a bronze basin for Aaron and his sons to wash their hands and feet so they do not die, and a holy anointing oil of myrrh, cinnamon, cane, cassia and olive oil for consecrating the Tent of Meeting, its furnishings, and the priests.
